contests.name: Ethernaut: Fallback
contests.gt_note: Hand-written from the public OpenZeppelin Ethernaut level descriptions, not from an audit report. Solutions are public and likely in model training data: plumbing checks only, never a quality metric.

official_findings.title: Ownership transfer via fallback function with minimal ETH contribution
official_findings.description: The receive() fallback checks msg.value > 0 and contributions[msg.sender] > 0, then transfers ownership. An attacker first calls contribute() with 1 wei, then sends 1 wei directly to claim ownership and drain the contract.

contests.name: Ethernaut: Fallout
contests.gt_note: Hand-written from the public OpenZeppelin Ethernaut level descriptions, not from an audit report. Solutions are public and likely in model training data: plumbing checks only, never a quality metric.

official_findings.title: Constructor typo allows anyone to become owner
official_findings.description: The contract has a function named Fal1out() (not Fallout) which was intended as the constructor. In Solidity < 0.5.0 this means it is a public function anyone can call to claim ownership. Calling Fal1out() sets owner = msg.sender.

contests.name: Ethernaut: Coin Flip
contests.gt_note: Hand-written from the public OpenZeppelin Ethernaut level descriptions, not from an audit report. Solutions are public and likely in model training data: plumbing checks only, never a quality metric.

official_findings.title: On-chain randomness via block.number is predictable
official_findings.description: The 'random' coin side is computed as block.number / FACTOR. An attacker contract can replicate this exact computation in the same block, always predicting the correct side and winning every flip.

official_findings.title: tx.origin vs msg.sender confusion allows ownership theft
official_findings.description: The ownership check is tx.origin != msg.sender. An attacker deploys an intermediary contract that calls changeOwner(), so tx.origin = attacker EOA while msg.sender = attacker contract. The condition is satisfied and ownership transfers to the attacker.

official_findings.title: Integer underflow in transfer() allows minting unlimited tokens
official_findings.description: balances[msg.sender] -= _value uses unchecked arithmetic (Solidity 0.6). If _value > balances[msg.sender], the uint256 underflows to a very large number. Attacker transfers more tokens than they own, resulting in a near-max-uint256 balance.
